label: Visual
title:
1.1 · Visual — every model, in one bay: attractors, maps, solids, geometry and sequences drawn in three dimensions, and the scope pictures, embeddings and audio displays drawn from a signal. The outer ring of the MODEL knob picks which kind, the inner ring which model, and the bank beside it is reprogrammed to that model's constants

The head of the row: the monitor, the knob that chooses which of this category's models is playing, its integration step, and anything that belongs to the category rather than to one model. Each model with constants of its own has a card of its own further along the row.

controls.label: λ  --
controls.title: 1.1.1 · Monitor — this bay's screen. It shows the model while this bay is the one driving the rack, and stands by when another is: only one model is drawn, so only one screen can carry a picture. The Screen switch under it cuts the copy out of the drawing buffer that the picture costs.

label: Visual · Model
title: 1.3 · Visual · Model — a bank of 28 programmable controls: the MODEL knob, then every constant, pot and selector of the model it is set to. Each display names what the control under it does for that model; turning the MODEL knob reprograms them, and each model keeps its own settings while another is showing. With Back on (Layers · Colors) they are the backdrop's.

controls.label: a
controls.title:
Rossler — a — a constant of the Rossler system. It enters
dy/dt = x + a·y

controls.label: σ
controls.title:
1.3.2 · Lorenz — σ — a constant of the Lorenz system. It enters
dx/dt = σ·(y - x)

controls.label: sys
controls.title: Sprott A–S — the system the MODEL knob's Sprott A–S position plays

controls.label: sweep
controls.title: SWEEP — which parameter of the system being swept is the x axis of the diagram; each column integrates the system fresh at that value and plots the maxima of z. The system is the most recent flow mode.

controls.label: solid
controls.title: Built-in solids — the rack modules and the 19-inch frame at their real dimensions, the geometry as closed solids, and every attractor swept as a tube along its own trajectory. Generated in the browser; the same models are written as .stl files by chaosrack stlgen.

controls.label: prog
controls.title: Program — which terminal program runs on the quad. Twenty-one animations plus the text demos, from tuiwasm; the list is built from what is registered, so it cannot drift from what is actually there.

controls.label: style
controls.title: Desktop style — four 3-D desktops reproduced over the scene. Flat: ordinary windows. Looking Glass (Sun, 2003): windows lean back in a legible stack; double-click a title bar to turn one over and read its back. Cube (Compiz, 2006): four workspaces on the faces of a cube; the arrow keys spin it. Metisse (2004): shift-drag a title bar to turn a window freely, and it stays live while turned. BumpTop (2009): windows have weight and fall into a pile on top of the rack.

controls.label: τ
controls.title: Takens Embedding — tau — the delay between the coordinates, in samples at 48 kHz, so one position is the same duration on any source. Too short and the axes are nearly the same sample and the figure collapses onto the diagonal; too long and it folds back on itself. One knob: Takens, Polar and the recurrence plot all read it.

controls.label: b
controls.title:
Rossler — b — a constant of the Rossler system. It enters
dz/dt = b + z·(x - c)

controls.label: ρ
controls.title:
1.4.1 · Lorenz — ρ — a constant of the Lorenz system. It enters
dy/dt = x·(ρ - z) - y

controls.label: drive
controls.title: DRIVE — what puts the system at a parameter value. sweep is the diagram alone, computed left to right. audio keeps the same diagram and points a cursor at it from the live audio envelope, so the branch structure under the music is lit up as it plays. The diagram itself does not move: its x axis means something only because the parameter runs monotonically along it. The envelope is the rack's signal, as the Mixer's RACK rows make it, and choosing audio is enough to start measuring it.

controls.label: smth
controls.title: Takens Embedding — smooth — Catmull-Rom upsampling, in drawn points per source sample. A straight line between samples draws chords that are an artifact of the drawing; this curves the beam through them instead. Higher is smoother and costs vertices.

controls.label: c
controls.title:
Rossler — c — a constant of the Rossler system. It enters
dz/dt = b + z·(x - c)

controls.label: β
controls.title:
1.4.2 · Lorenz — β — a constant of the Lorenz system. It enters
dz/dt = x·y - β·z

controls.label: wave
controls.title: Wave — the carrier waveform: square, pulse, or a sub-octave square (divided by two)

controls.label: mod
controls.title: Mod — the modulator topology: ring (four-quadrant) or AM (balanced)

controls.label: spd
controls.title: 1.12.1 · Model Out SPD — how fast the model runs as a signal, in semitones: every 12 up is twice as fast, an octave higher. For a system of equations, integrator steps per sample, 0 being one step a sample; the pitch is the system's own. For a beam, its speed round the figure, so the pitch is that speed over the figure's length, which the HZ readout over the equation shows.

controls.label: lvl
controls.title: 1.12.2 · Model Out LVL — the level of the model's x, y and z, as the Mixer takes them (0–100).

controls.label: speed
controls.title: 1.12.3 · SPEED — the model's time base, at 1.12.3 below Model Out. For a flow it sets integration sub-steps per drawn vertex above ×1, and scales dt below ×1; for an animated model (Lissajous, turtle, pong, morph) it sets the playback rate. Dark for models with no time base of their own (geometry, maps, analysis displays).

label: Record
title: 2.1 · Record — a monitor showing exactly what will be captured, and the transport that captures it. The picture is the recorded area, not the whole canvas, so what you see here is what lands in the file.

The picture is a copy out of the model's own drawing buffer every frame, which is not free; the rack shows every module in a bay now, so a screen you are not watching needs a switch of its own rather than relying on the module being put away. Off, the glass goes dark and the module costs nothing.

controls.label: Zoom
controls.title: 2.4.3 · Zoom, and Fore nested on top of it. ZOOM is the camera's distance, on a knob that turns once round like the position knobs, its readout in degrees of that turn. FORE is where the model sits relative to the rack, as a moving partition rather than a switch. Fully back and all of it is behind the controls; fully forward and all of it is in front; anywhere between and the panel cuts through it, near half in front and far half behind. The cut is a plane parallel to the screen, so it stays put as you turn the model. A flat picture — the spectrogram, the terminal — has no depth to cut, so it moves whole. The reset puts both back.

label: Grid
title: 2.5 · Grid — how many views of the model are drawn, what differs between them, and which of them the knobs are pointed at. It sits in the DISPLAY bay beside View and Position because it is a question about the picture, not about the signal: Trace is how one trajectory is drawn, View is where the camera is, and this is how many cameras there are.

controls.label: grid
controls.title: 2.5.1 · Grid — how many views of the model are drawn, as a square (2 is side by side). A grid is not that many instruments configured by hand: pick what varies with the Sweep dial and the cells draw that parameter's range, which is a contact sheet of one setting rather than sixteen panels to fill in.

controls.label: sweep
controls.title: 2.5.2 · Sweep — which parameter varies across the grid, and the from and to knobs beside this one say over how much of its range. This is what makes a grid of sixteen usable: rather than sixteen panels to fill in, one dial says what differs and the cells draw that parameter's space, like a contact sheet. The list is the CURRENT model's own parameters, so it changes with the mode; a model that integrates its trajectory offers no parameter sweep, because the cells share one integrator and a swept grid would smear one trajectory across them. A flow offers start instead: each cell integrates its own trajectory, started ε from the model's own. csrc and cmap sweep the COLORING instead of a number — the same figure read nine different ways, or in nine palettes — which is the case a grid is most worth having for.

controls.label: down
controls.title: 2.5.3 · Sweep down — a SECOND parameter, varying down the grid while the first varies across it. This is what the second direction of a grid is for: with one sweep a three by three of nine delays wasted its rows, and asking for nine palettes meant giving up the nine delays. Set both and each column is one value of across, each row one value of down, and the cell where they meet is the pair — nine delays read in three palettes, say. Set only this one and it behaves exactly like the sweep beside it. The two cannot name the same parameter: rows and columns varying the same thing is not a comparison.

controls.label: from
controls.title: 2.6.1 · Sweep from — where in the swept parameter's own range the first cell sits, as a fraction: 0 is the parameter's minimum. Turn both this and to inward and the contact sheet covers a slice of the range in detail rather than all of it coarsely, which is how a sweep is used once you know roughly where the interesting part is. For a start sweep the fraction sets ε: 0 is ε = 0, the model's own trajectory, and above 0 the scale is logarithmic, 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻¹.

positions.title: 0 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
1 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: to
controls.title: 2.6.2 · Sweep to — where in the swept parameter's own range the last cell sits, as a fraction: 1 is the parameter's maximum. Below the from knob and the sweep runs backwards, which is worth having when the interesting end should be read first.

positions.title: 0 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
1 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: focus
controls.title: 2.6.3 · Focus — which cell of the grid the knobs drive while Link is off. Its positions follow the grid, so a sixteen-cell sheet has sixteen of them. Moving it rebuilds the parameter rows against that cell's own instance, which is what makes a knob write to the view you are looking at rather than to the one behind it.

label: Display
title: 2.7 · Display — trace rendering: line width, point decimation, trail length and mode, and the overlays drawn on the trace (Poincaré section, graticule). Three P-units; the switches are on their buttons. The twin trajectory is now the Grid's start sweep with Overlay on.

controls.label: line
controls.title: 2.7.1 · LINE — trace line width, 1 to 10 pixels. Buttons: S Poincaré section, G graticule; each is an independent switch.

positions.title: 1 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
10 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: points
controls.title: 2.7.2 · POINTS — point decimation. At 0 the trace is a solid line. Any other setting draws the trace as that many points, evenly spaced along it; a setting at or above the trail's vertex count is equivalent to a solid line. Useful where the figure folds over itself and a solid line obscures its structure.

positions.title: 0 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise

positions.title: 4k — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: trail
controls.title: 2.7.3 · TRAIL — trail length, in vertices, and trail mode. The buttons select the mode: persist, scan or ring.

label: Layers · Colors
title: 2.8 · Layers · Colors — how the picture is made up and colored. BEHIND draws a second picture filling the canvas behind the model and SKIN paints one onto its surface; BG is the color behind it all. SRC is what the color follows, MAP how a value becomes a color, PERIOD and SHIFT the window on the map, TRAIL how much of the trail stays lit, and START, MID and END the gradient's own colors. The switches: FILL makes the spectrogram or FVF plane the whole screen face-on, INVERT reverses the gradient, HELD stops the color range refitting itself.

controls.label: behind
controls.title: 2.8.1 · Backdrop — what is drawn behind the model, filling the canvas: the scrolling spectrogram, the XY oscilloscope, a live terminal, or the whole desk. Water is the exception: it is a LENS, drawn through the finished frame rather than behind it — drag on the canvas to make waves. One at a time, or off.

controls.label: skin
controls.title: 2.8.2 · Skin — what is painted ON the model's own surface, wrapped round it, for the models that have a surface to take it: the live spectrogram, a terminal, or the whole desk. Off leaves the wireframe. The same three pictures the Behind knob draws in the background; this puts one on the object instead.

controls.label: bg
controls.title: 2.8.3 · Background color behind the model — swatch or Hue / Level knob

controls.label: start
controls.title: 2.9.1 · Gradient START color (low end of the source axis) — pick with the swatch or dial it with the Hue (outer) / Level (inner) knob

controls.label: mid
controls.title: 2.9.2 · Gradient MIDDLE color (3-color palette only) — swatch or Hue / Level knob

controls.label: end
controls.title: 2.9.3 · Gradient END color (high end of the source axis) — swatch or Hue / Level knob

controls.label: src
controls.title: 2.10.1 · Source — what the color follows. OFF is a flat trace in the start swatch: the color follows nothing, which is what used to be called the mono palette and is a statement about the SOURCE rather than about the map. X / Y / Z follow a coordinate of the figure; on the three delay embeddings those axes are one signal at three lags, so they color along different directions of the same figure rather than showing three different quantities. TRAIL follows age along the window. AUDIO paints the short-time spectral CENTROID along the trail — which frequency each moment sits at. LEVEL paints the short-time LEVEL instead, which is the quantity the spectrogram backdrop is painting, so with one of the colormap palettes behind it the figure and the backdrop say the same thing in the same language; AUDIO deliberately does not, and a figure colored by centroid over a spectrogram is not supposed to match it. Only the Takens, stereo and polar embeddings have a trail that is a time axis, so elsewhere both are one flat tint. Displays with a value of their own — the spectrogram, the RTA, the transfer function — do not consult this knob at all, and it dims in those modes.

controls.label: map
controls.title: 2.10.2 · Map — how a value becomes a color, for every display in the rack including the spectrogram. 2 and 3 mix the Palette module's own swatches; HUE is a raw hue sweep; heat, blue, gray, turbo, viridis and magma are the published colormaps. Turbo and viridis are the even ones — equal steps in the value look like equal steps in color, which a hue sweep does not give you. This is the only colormap control there is: the spectrogram had a second one naming the same six maps, and two knobs that had to be kept in step by hand were one knob too many.

controls.label: period
controls.title: 2.10.3 · Palette period — how many times the palette is crossed across the trail (low = a narrow slice of it, which the shift knob then sweeps). Drives the rainbow AND the six colormaps: the question is the same one either way.

positions.title: 0.05 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
20 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: shift
controls.title: 2.11.1 · Palette shift — where the window sits on the colormap. Turn the period down to a slice and this sweeps that slice along heat / blue / gray / turbo / viridis / magma; route it from audio in the Mod module and the sound moves the figure THROUGH the map instead of only tinting it. Past either end the map turns back rather than wrapping — turbo's two ends are different colors, and joining them puts a hard seam across the figure — so ±1 is the reversed map, not a dead stop.

positions.title: -1 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
1 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

label: Lattice
title: 3.1 · Lattice — any model drawn in depth by terminals. Each sheet of the stack is a real terminal running [lattice](https://github.com/0magnet/lattice), and each draws its own slice of the volume: with the Lattice model, its solid; with L lit on ROWS, the model chosen, whatever it is. The model's trail, mesh or dots are the figure every program is handed, and a voxel is lit where the figure passes through it, written as the way the figure runs across the sheet. The model keeps its own knobs in the bank, so it is played as ever; these six are how the lattice draws it. Pictures and terminals, which are flat already, are not drawn in it.

controls.label: rows
controls.title: 3.1.1 · ROWS — each terminal's height in rows, which is its resolution: the programs read their terminal's size, as programs do, and draw that many voxels across. A family has as many sheets as a terminal has rows, so this is the volume's resolution in all three dimensions: more rows is a terminal zoomed out to smaller characters, and a finer volume. 3 × rows terminals of 2 × rows columns; finer costs more. Button: L draws the model chosen in the lattice.

positions.title: 6 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
24 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: style
controls.title: 3.1.2 · STYLE — how each terminal writes what crosses its sheet.

controls.label: look
controls.title: 3.1.3 · LOOK — how the sheets are put together on screen.

controls.label: opac
controls.title: 3.2.1 · OPAC — every terminal's background opacity, in percent: the setting a translucent terminal emulator has (kitty's background_opacity, alacritty's window.opacity), never something a program asks for. It applies to the default background, which is black; text stays opaque. At 0 only the text is there; higher, each sheet darkens what is behind it, so the far side is dimmer than the near.

positions.title: 0 — the lowest this knob goes; turned fully counter-clockwise
100 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: stacks
controls.title: 3.2.2 · STACKS — which families of sheets there are. Fewer families are fewer terminals and less to draw: a family that is not shown does not run its programs either.

controls.label: turn

label: Spectro
title: 3.3 · Spectro — the spectrogram's own controls, wherever it is: the model (Spectrogram, or FVF's surface), the skin painted on a surface, or the backdrop filling the canvas behind the model. They are in this module for all three, and live in any of them; with no spectrogram on screen their readouts are blank.

controls.title: 3.3.1 · DFT size — points per transform: larger resolves frequency finer and time coarser.

controls.label: ovlp
controls.title: 3.3.2 · overlap — how much each transform overlaps the one before, in percent: more is a smoother scroll for more work.

controls.label: wfn
controls.title: 3.3.3 · window function — the taper each block is shaped by before its transform: Hann is the usual; rectangular is sharpest and leaks the most.

controls.label: chan
controls.title: 3.4.1 · channel — which signal is analyzed: the mix of both, or the left or right alone.

controls.label: scale
controls.title: 3.4.2 · scale — the magnitude scale: logarithmic, in dB, or linear. FLOOR and CEILING are read in the same scale.

controls.label: min
controls.title: 3.4.3 · floor — the level, in dB, that maps to the bottom of the color scale; anything quieter is drawn black.

controls.label: max
controls.title: 3.5.1 · ceiling — the level, in dB, that maps to the top of the color scale; anything louder is drawn at full.

label: Section
title: 3.6 · Where the Poincaré section's plane sits, and which way through it counts. ON (on AXIS) switches the section on over a running flow, as LINE's S does; the knobs are live over a flow while it is on, and always under Analysis → Poincaré Section, whose plane they are. AXIS and POS place it — POS as a fraction of the attractor's own reach along that axis, so 0 is through the middle whatever the system's size. DIR one way is the default: a bounded flow that goes up through a plane must come back down through it, so counting both superimposes two different sections. The crossings draw in gold where they physically are; Analysis → Poincaré Section is the same section as a picture of its own, with the return map.

controls.label: axis
controls.title: 3.6.1 · axis — the axis the section plane is perpendicular to.

controls.label: pos
controls.title: 3.6.2 · pos — where the plane sits along AXIS, as a fraction of the attractor's own reach: 0 is through the middle whatever the system's size.

controls.label: dir
controls.title: 3.6.3 · dir — which way through the plane counts as a crossing. One way is the default because a bounded flow that goes up through a plane must come back down, and keeping both superimposes two different sections.

label: Water
title: 3.7 · The water lens's tank: the finished picture seen through a rippling surface. Drag across the picture to make a wake; DRIVE lets the sound push the water from SPKRS points, and RAIN drops on it at random. Its knobs are live while BEHIND is on water, and can be set before it is.

controls.label: bend
controls.title: 3.7.1 · bend — how far the surface's slope moves the picture behind it. Zero is clear glass, whatever the water does.

controls.label: speed
controls.title: 3.7.2 · speed — how fast a ripple crosses the tank.

controls.label: damp
controls.title: 3.7.3 · damp — how much of a wave survives each step, in thousandths: 990 rings for seconds, 900 dies before it crosses.

controls.label: visc
controls.title: 3.8.1 · viscosity — smooths the surface each step, so fine ripples fade before broad ones.

controls.label: walls
controls.title: 3.8.2 · walls — how much of a wave the edges send back, in percent. 100 is a tank with its own echoes; 0 is open water.

controls.label: drive
controls.title: 3.8.3 · drive — how hard the sound pushes the surface. Zero leaves it to the pointer and the rain.

controls.label: spkrs
controls.title: 3.9.1 · speakers — how many points in the tank the sound pushes from, spread round a circle.

controls.label: rain
controls.title: 3.9.2 · rain — drops a second, falling at random.

label: Physics
title: 3.10 · The figure as a rigid body in the plane of the screen, inside a room whose walls are the edges of the picture. ON (on GRAV) switches it on; the knobs are live while it is on and the Turtle Path is running. GRAV pulls either way up; FRIC is how much the surfaces bite; BOUNCE is how much of the speed a wall gives back; SPIN is how readily it turns.

controls.label: grav
controls.title: 3.10.1 · gravity — pull in world units per second squared; below zero lifts.

controls.label: fric
controls.title: 3.10.2 · friction — how much the figure is slowed where it touches.

controls.label: bounce
controls.title: 3.10.3 · bounce — how much of its speed the figure keeps off a wall.

controls.label: spin
controls.title: 3.11.1 · spin — how hard the figure is to turn.

controls.label: MIDI
controls.title: 3.12.1.c · WebMIDI — hardware control: CC 1..N drive the current mode's parameter knobs in order, CC 21..28 the view targets (zoom, pans, spins, rainbow, trail), and any note hops to that note's attractor.

controls.label: Power
controls.title: 3.12.1.d · Power — the render loop. Off stops it and clears the canvas, which is what the GPU costs; the panel stays, so every setting is still there to read and to change. A switch again, and back in the Rack group where the rest of the frame's own controls are: it had been folded into the model knob's first detent, which made powering down look like choosing a model called OFF and put the rack's power switch inside the one control that had nothing to do with the rack.

controls.label: Rack bay
controls.title: 3.12.2.a · Rack bay — draw the 19-inch frame each ROW of modules sits in: rails above and below, an ear each side, and blank panels filling the leftover at the end of the row on the same slot pitch. The modules wrap, and a row is a bay, so a rack that has spilled onto a second row gets a second frame. Handles and panel screws are chosen on the Style module: the inner ring of Size.

The scene keeps running behind. Open a terminal, the host shell or the file manager from the desk's Applications menu. The OTHER way to have the desk is as a MODEL (Solids → desk), where the whole desktop is drawn into the scene and turns with it.

label: Distortion
title: 4.4 · Distortion — THD, THD+N, SINAD and ENOB of the live audio, measured against whichever tone is in it. Feed it a generator's sine at 1 kHz (type 1000 into its Hz readout) through whatever you want measured and read how much of what comes back is not that tone. THD is the harmonics alone, which is the number a specification quotes; THD+N is everything that is not the fundamental, which is the honest one and always the larger; SINAD is the same ratio in decibels, the way a converter is specified; ENOB runs the ideal-converter relation backwards and says how many bits would sound this clean. The gap between THD and THD+N is how much of the rubbish is hiss rather than distortion. The instrument's own floor is about 0.0015% THD+N (96.5 dB SINAD, 17.3 effective bits), measured on a synthesized pure tone — that is the Blackman-Harris window's leakage past the notch, and nothing quieter than it can be read.

label: Loudness
title: 4.6 · Loudness — LUFS to ITU-R BS.1770 and EBU R 128, the scale everything is delivered against. M is the momentary loudness over 400 ms, S the short-term over 3 s, I the INTEGRATED reading over everything since the last reset — gated, so silence and quiet passages do not drag a programme's number down, which is what makes it the number a delivery spec means. LRA is the loudness range, how far the loud parts sit above the quiet ones: one number for how dynamic the material is, and the thing a loudness target alone says nothing about. TP is the TRUE peak in dBTP, the peak of the reconstructed signal rather than of the samples — a full-scale tone at a quarter of the sample rate can have every sample at −3 dBFS and still clip the converter, which is why a delivery ceiling is a true-peak ceiling. K-weighting is derived from the analog prototype at whatever rate the audio is arriving at, not the 48 kHz coefficients the standard prints, so the weighting is the same filter at every rate.

label: Wow & Flutter
title: 4.7 · Wow & Flutter — speed stability, measured off a 3150 Hz test tone. Every other analyzer here asks about amplitude; this asks whether the TIME AXIS is steady, which is what a turntable, a tape deck or a cassette is judged by. Play a generator's sine at 3150 Hz through the deck, capture the result, and read it here: SPEED is the mean frequency error as a percentage (a constant error is a pitch shift, a different fault from a wobble), WOW the slow 0.5–6 Hz modulation that once-per-revolution faults produce, FLUTTER the fast 6–100 Hz kind from capstans and idlers, and W&F the DIN-weighted quasi-peak that a specification quotes — the deviation through a filter peaked at 4 Hz, where the ear is most sensitive to pitch movement. 3150 Hz is the figure every test record carries (DIN 45507, IEC 60386). With no deck in the loop at all it reads 0.000% on the generator itself, which is the check that the instrument is not inventing the number.

title: 4.9 · Features — what the Mod matrix's audio routes read, as a meter bridge: six LED bar graphs, one for each feature of the incoming audio's mono mix, the same numbers a route modulates a knob by. Each ladder is twenty segments, green to 70%, amber to 90% and red above. The levels are relative, not absolute: each feature is scaled by its own recent peak (instant rise, slow fall), so a quiet passage still fills the ladders and a loud one does not pin them. Dark while modulation is off — nothing routed and no feed from the server — since then nothing is measured. They were a strip over the top-left of the picture with a switch to hide it; as a module they are on the rack beside the other meters, and off the picture.

label: Timing
title: 4.10 · Timing — the rack metering itself. FRAME is the average interval in milliseconds and FPS its reciprocal, taken over the mean rather than the median so one hesitation a second cannot hide behind fifty-nine good frames. MIN and MAX are the best and worst frame in the window. LATE is the share of frames that missed the display's own interval, which is measured rather than assumed: nothing renders faster than vsync, so the shortest frame in a window IS the interval, and the reading means the same on a 60 Hz panel and a 144 Hz one. The four figures below it are where the frame went — MODEL the passes that draw the instrument, METERS everything the rack does to its own audio, SCOPE the tube, and REST the browser's own style, layout, raster and compositing, which is usually the largest share of the four. A rack that draws in 4 ms and spends 9 ms measuring its own audio is not slow, it is mis-apportioned, and no single frame rate says so.

controls.title: 4.10.1.a · Timing / fps / LED readout / Frames a second sustained over the last window — the reciprocal of the MEAN frame, so a hitch counts against it
4.10.1.c · Timing / min / LED readout / Shortest frame in the window, in ms — which is the display's own interval, since nothing renders faster than vsync

4.10.2.b · Timing / late / LED readout / Percentage of frames that missed the display's interval by half again or more. This is the number that corresponds to visible hesitation; the frame rate alone does not.

4.10.3.a · Timing / model / LED readout / Milliseconds a frame spent ISSUING the model's draw calls. A WebGL call queues a command and returns without waiting for pixels, so this reads far below what the model really costs — the GPU and compositor share of it is in REST. Useful for what it does catch: geometry rebuilt every frame instead of cached.

controls.label: TBC
controls.title: 4.10.3.c · TBC — timebase correction. On, the model turns at its rate per SECOND: each frame advances it by however long that frame took, so a late frame is a longer step and a faster display the same speed. Off, every frame advances it the same step, as the rack did before: a late frame is a pause, and a 144 Hz display spins it more than twice as fast as a 60 Hz one. On is the steady angular velocity; off is every frame advanced alike, which is what to compare frames by.

label: Scope 1
title: 5.1 · Scope 1 — one of the rack's four oscilloscopes, each beside its generator. Under VOLTS and TIME, the INPUT knobs 1 and 2, each beside a display naming its source, pick what each input is fed from — the rack's signal (RACK L or R, as the Mixer makes it), the capture (CAP L or R, wherever the Mixer sends it), one generator by itself, or a coordinate of the model (Model Out) — named on the face. The tube, and at its right the SOURCE buttons — what the beam draws: IN 1, IN 2, the two summed (SUM), or one against the other (X-Y) — between the small H and V knobs that move the trace sideways and up and down. Under it the beam's knob: its outer ring is SCALE ILLUM, which lights the graticule and, turned down past the bottom of its travel, clicks into OFF and switches the scope off; inside it INTENSITY, and innermost FOCUS. Beside that the TRIGGER, with its SLOPE and MODE buttons, and below them VOLTS and TIME, how much a division is worth up and across.

label: Gen 1

5.3 · Gen 1 — a generator, for sound or for modulation. The FREQ knob, an encoder with no stops — a click a semitone, a turn an octave, the ring's color which octave — from 0.107 Hz up to 28160 Hz, over a piano octave; the level knob inside its envelope's ATTACK and DECAY rings, with ENV between them to repeat it; and the waveform knob, OFF at the bottom, with SOLO beside it to hear only this one and OUT under it.

Where it goes is OUT: OFF, L, C (both sides) or R, on the speakers and the rack's signal together. The Mixer's GEN 1 column has every other pinning — the speakers or the rack alone, a gain, an inverted side, the sends to modulation — and OUT reads MIX while it does.

label: Scope 2
title: 5.4 · Scope 2 — one of the rack's four oscilloscopes, each beside its generator. Under VOLTS and TIME, the INPUT knobs 1 and 2, each beside a display naming its source, pick what each input is fed from — the rack's signal (RACK L or R, as the Mixer makes it), the capture (CAP L or R, wherever the Mixer sends it), one generator by itself, or a coordinate of the model (Model Out) — named on the face. The tube, and at its right the SOURCE buttons — what the beam draws: IN 1, IN 2, the two summed (SUM), or one against the other (X-Y) — between the small H and V knobs that move the trace sideways and up and down. Under it the beam's knob: its outer ring is SCALE ILLUM, which lights the graticule and, turned down past the bottom of its travel, clicks into OFF and switches the scope off; inside it INTENSITY, and innermost FOCUS. Beside that the TRIGGER, with its SLOPE and MODE buttons, and below them VOLTS and TIME, how much a division is worth up and across.

controls.label: inten
controls.title: 5.4.2 · The beam. The knob is INTENSITY: beam brightness, and how long the phosphor holds the trace. Under it, two mini knobs. I is SCALE ILLUM, which lights the graticule; turned down past the bottom of its travel it clicks into OFF and switches the scope off — the tube goes dark and costs the rack nothing. F is FOCUS: how tight the spot is; off focus the trace blurs, the way a real tube does. The display reads the intensity, or whichever mini knob is being turned.

controls.label: trig
controls.title: 5.5.2 · Trigger — LEVEL is the value the signal must cross, in the SLOPE direction, for a sweep to start; set it inside the waveform or nothing triggers. SLOPE, the buttons at the right: + triggers on the signal rising through the level, − on it falling. MODE, the buttons at the left: AUTO sweeps anyway when nothing crosses, so silence shows a baseline; NORM sweeps only on a trigger and holds the last trace otherwise.

5.5.2 · 1 — the highest this knob goes; turned fully clockwise

controls.label: volts
controls.title: 5.4.3 · Volts/div — how much signal one division of height is worth, detented 1-2-5. A trace off the top of the screen means this is set too fine. Under it INPUT 1, a mini knob with a display of its own: what input 1 is fed from — the rack's L or R, the capture's L or R, Gen 1 to 4 alone, or the model's x, y or z — named on that display, which lists them all when clicked, and on the face, top left. INPUT 2 is under TIME. The reset puts both back.

controls.label: time
controls.title: 5.5.3 · Time/div — how long the beam takes to cross one division; ten divisions is the whole screen. Under it INPUT 2, what input 2 is fed from, as INPUT 1 is under VOLTS. The reset puts both back.
